common_name: Newe Ya'ar No. 4 Sage (High-Oil Israeli Culinary Sage)

planting.note: Propagate only from rooted cuttings or division of the selected clone, since seed-grown plants will not reliably reproduce the elevated essential-oil content this line was selected for; set out in spring once soil has warmed.

directions: Set rooted cuttings or divisions into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun and avoid overwatering, since excess moisture dilutes the oil concentration this clone was bred to maximize. Newe Ya'ar No. 4 is a selected culinary sage line developed by Israeli agricultural researchers specifically for consistently high essential-oil yield in commercial distillation and dried-herb production, rather than for ornamental leaf color or flower display. The gray-green leaves and habit closely resemble common culinary sage, but the plant is grown primarily where a dependable, laboratory-verified oil chemotype matters more than novelty. Cut back hard after flowering to encourage dense new growth and harvest leaves for drying just before bloom, when oil content peaks.

planting.note: Propagate from softwood cuttings taken in late spring or early summer, since this variegated selection does not come true from seed; plant out once rooted and hardened off.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; a touch of afternoon shade in hot climates helps the leaf variegation stay crisp rather than scorching. Woodcote is a compact culinary sage cultivar whose new growth emerges cream and soft pink before maturing to gray-green, giving a softer, pastel-toned variegation pattern than the older, bolder Tricolor sage. The leaves carry the same savory culinary sage flavor as green cultivars and can be used interchangeably in cooking. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mound tidy and encourage the flush of freshly colored new leaves that make this cultivar distinctive.

common_name: Kew Gold Sage (Solid Golden-Leaved Culinary Sage)

planting.note: Propagate by cuttings or division in spring; this selected sport does not breed true from seed and is maintained clonally in the nursery trade.

directions: Grow in well-drained, low-fertility soil in full sun, where strong light intensifies the leaf color; too much shade or overly rich soil causes the gold tone to fade toward green. Kew Gold is a low, mounding culinary sage selection with solid, even yellow-gold foliage that holds its color through the season more reliably than older gold-splashed selections such as Aurea, and it rarely flowers, keeping energy focused on leaf production. The flavor and aroma match standard culinary sage and the leaves can be harvested and used the same way. Its compact, non-flowering habit suits edging and container use as much as the kitchen garden.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost once nights are reliably mild; in cold climates grow in a container and bring under cover for winter, as this trailing form is less hardy than upright rosemary cultivars.

directions: Plant in fast-draining soil in full sun, ideally on a slope, wall, or raised bed where the trailing stems can cascade freely. Pinkie is a low, spreading rosemary selection distinguished from most other trailing rosemary cultivars by its soft pink flowers rather than the usual blue or violet, blooming heavily in cooler months. The narrow, dark green leaves have the same pungent culinary aroma as upright rosemary and are fully usable in cooking. Because it is more cold-sensitive than hardier upright types, protect container-grown plants from hard freezes or treat it as a seasonal ornamental-culinary plant in colder zones.

common_name: Shady Acres Rosemary (Tall Upright Culinary Hedge Rosemary)

planting.note: Transplant rooted cuttings after the last frost in full sun; this upright cultivar tolerates light shearing well, making it suitable for hedging once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants for a hedge line if grown as a boundary planting. Shady Acres is a vigorous, strongly upright rosemary cultivar that grows noticeably taller and narrower than many culinary rosemary selections, making it a popular choice for tall herbal hedges and topiary rather than groundcover use. The narrow, dark green leaves carry the classic strong culinary rosemary flavor and can be harvested year-round in mild climates. Light pale-blue flowers appear mainly in winter and spring; prune after flowering to maintain a dense, upright form.

common_name: Aureum Crispum Oregano (Curly Golden Culinary Oregano)

planting.note: Divide established clumps or plant rooted divisions in spring; the crinkled golden leaf form is maintained vegetatively rather than from seed.

directions: Plant divisions in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; strong light keeps the foliage a bright gold rather than fading toward green. Aureum Crispum is a low, mat-forming golden oregano distinguished from the smooth-leaved Golden Oregano by its tightly crinkled, crimped leaf texture, giving the mound a ruffled, almost mossy appearance. The leaves carry a milder oregano flavor than green culinary types but are still usable fresh in small amounts. Shear back after flowering to renew the compact habit and refresh leaf color for the following season.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring in full sun; the golden leaf color is a clonal selection and is not reproduced reliably from seed.

directions: Grow in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage color is most vivid in full sun but the plant tolerates light shade better than most golden-leaved herbs. Norton's Gold forms a low, rounded mound of smooth, bright yellow-gold leaves that stay more evenly colored through summer heat than many golden oregano selections, which tend to green up as temperatures rise. Small pale pink flower clusters appear in mid to late summer, adding a second season of interest without detracting from the foliage display. Trim lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and encourage fresh gold new growth.

common_name: Nanum Dwarf Oregano (Compact Non-Flowering Edging Oregano)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun; this dwarf form is propagated vegetatively to keep the compact, tightly mounded habit true.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, such as a rock garden pocket, trough, or path edging. Nanum is a miniature form of common oregano that forms a dense, tight mound only a few inches tall, rarely producing the flower spikes typical of full-sized oregano, so its appeal is as a neat, low edging plant rather than a flowering ornamental. The tiny, aromatic leaves have a milder version of standard oregano flavor and can be snipped sparingly for cooking. Its slow, compact growth means it needs little pruning beyond an occasional trim to keep the mound even.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Kemper Center for Home Gardening

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or cuttings in spring in full sun; this naturally occurring hybrid is maintained clonally rather than grown from seed.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; like most thymes it resents heavy, wet soil and performs best in rock gardens, path edging, or containers. Longwood is a naturally occurring hybrid thyme first identified at a botanical garden, prized for a strong, resinous, camphor-and-thyme scent that is more pungent than common culinary thyme when the foliage is brushed or crushed. The small, narrow leaves form a low, wiry mound topped with pale lavender-pink flowers favored by pollinators in summer. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mound dense and to prevent the center from opening up and going woody.
